passages.quote:
This section explains how to recognise, report, and manage outbreaks and incidents in adult social care settings. Effective management helps reduce the spread of infection and protects the health, wellbeing, dignity, and safety of people accessing care and support, their families, and staff.

Key summary

an outbreak is usually 2 or more linked cases of the same infection that happen at the same time and in the same place

spot symptoms early to help stop the spread

report outbreaks quickly and work with partners (e.g. UKHSA local HPT, GPs, IPC teams)

use the right infection prevention and control measures

review and learn to improve future response

Call for action

be alert to symptoms and act quickly if more than one person is unwell

report outbreaks quickly through the right channels

follow the outbreak plan and infection control measures

keep staff, families, and partners informed

increase cleaning, hygiene, and PPE use

watch for new cases and act fast

balance infection control with people’s wellbeing

after the outbreak, deep clean, review, and update plans

ensure safer visiting guidance is followed

Managing outbreaks and incidents effectively in adult social care (ASC) settings is essential to protect the health, dignity and wellbeing of people who access care and support, their loved ones, as well as care and support workers, and healthcare practitioners.

People accessing care and support are often vulnerable to the effects of infectious diseases due to their age or underlying medical conditions, and outbreaks can spread quickly in ASC settings, with serious consequences. People accessing care and support and care and support workers are also more susceptible to infections that increase during winter months (respiratory and stomach infections) which can cause serious outbreaks due to close contact in communal ASC settings.

Good infection prevention and control (IPC) practices can help reduce the risk of outbreaks occurring.

This guidance is intended to support ASC providers in England to prevent, identify and manage infectious disease outbreaks. It sets out practical actions, roles and responsibilities, and key principles for working with UKHSA health protection teams (HPTs) and local partners such as local authorities, Integrated Care Boards (ICBs), Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) teams, GPs, pharmacies, and commissioners. The guidance aims to support proportionate, person-centred responses that balance IPC with people’s rights, wellbeing and quality of life.

Outbreaks and incidents are more common in care homes and other residential settings, where people and staff are in close contact with each other. However, they can also happen in domiciliary or home care, where they may be harder to spot. In these situations, keeping records of linked cases in different households can help identify an outbreak.

It is important to be clear when concerns should be raised and who is responsible for coordinating the response. Concerns should also be reported to the UKHSA local HPT or IPC team for advice and support.

Local HPTs can support with conducting a risk assessment for protecting people accessing care and support as well as care and support workers, to ensure safe care can be delivered. They can advise on the management of contacts in all ASC settings if required.

Safeguarding statement

In keeping with the Mental Capacity Act 2005, care and support workers must presume capacity unless assessed otherwise, provide tailored support to enable understanding, and document any capacity assessments clearly. Where a person lacks capacity, decisions or protective measures must be made in their best interests and be proportionate, necessary, and least restrictive, with involvement from relevant professionals and those close to the person wherever appropriate.

Always ensure any information sharing about a person who is infectious is done so in a compassionate but proportionate way.

Outbreak definition

An outbreak is when two or more people have the same infection and are linked in time and place or common exposure. This includes people accessing care and support and care and support workers.

It can also be when the number of infections appears unusual or higher than what is normally seen in an ASC setting (communal setting or domiciliary care). Other situations where outbreak procedures should be followed include:

when a single case of a rare infectious disease (for example, diphtheria, rabies, polio, botulism) or high-consequence diseases (such as a viral haemorrhagic fever) happens

when there has been suspected or confirmed contamination (for example, of food, water, medicines, or medical devices)

Recognising an outbreak early

Be alert to signs of infection and any changes in a person’s usual behaviour. Care and support workers are often the first to notice these subtle changes and symptoms of infection in people that they care for even when the person hasn’t said they feel unwell.

If more than one person under your care is experiencing similar symptoms it may indicate spread, even where there may be no obvious links. This also applies to domiciliary care, where people may not share living spaces but may be exposed to infection in the community. Rota patterns, sickness data and call logs may be useful to monitor and detect outbreaks and act early.

What to look for

During an outbreak, people may be experiencing similar symptoms, such as:

high temperature (usually 37.8 degrees Celsius or higher)

diarrhoea and/or vomiting

unexplained rash

cough, breathlessness or other respiratory symptoms

sudden confusion or unexpected falls

These are some of the common symptoms, but others may also occur. Symptoms may be present in care and support workers, and visitors as well as those accessing care.
